newsitem.title: USA: USDA Glickman-Look at new farm reserve appropriate.
newsitem.headline: USDA Glickman-Look at new farm reserve appropriate.

text.p: Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said it would be "appropriate" to consider creation of a new U.S. farmer-held reserve to bolster grain prices.
Glickman, who was speaking in a telephone news conference from the World Food Summit in Rome, also said he expected wheat prices would continue to strengthen.
He also said his discussions on the sidelines of the summit had found resistance to freer agricultural trade and reluctance to allow sales of genetically engineered foods.
"I come back from the conference recognizing that these problems (opposition to biofoods) certainly are more challenging than I went over there thinking they were," Glickman said.
The European Union has yet to decide whether to allow sale of a biocorn than produces a natural pesticide. An herbicide-tolerant soybean, also developed in the United States, has run into resistance.
The "Freedom to Farm" law enacted this year eliminated the long-term Farmer Owned Reserve, which paid a storage fee to farmers who wanted to delay marketing due to low grain prices.

"I sense that the wheat market is firming, and i think it will continue to firm. And I think to some extent, that's going to be true with the other markets, although maybe not so much as with wheat," Glickman told a reporter who asked if a long-term reserve should be created in view of recent price declines for corn and wheat.
"I do think it is appropriate to look at the area of reserves," he said, noting Senator Bob Kerrey, Nebraska Democrat, was "particularly interested" in the matter.
"I don't know what we'll come up with but I would be interested in working with Congress. And again, it has to be a bipartisan Congress or we won't get this thing done."

Glickman said, however, he did not want major revisions of the 1996 farm policy law. In addition to a look at "responsible reserves," he said areas for consideration were risk management tools, unduly harsh credit rules and landlord-tenant relations under "Freedom to Farm."
Some landlords were "basically icing their tenants out," he said. Bipartisan agreement was vital for action on all issues.
